Suppose we would like to find an integrating factor to convert the differential equation

$$
{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x+xy\,\text{d}y=0,\,y>0
$$

into an exact equation using an integrating factor. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
{{field-1}}=h(y)
$$

where $h(y)$ is independent of $x,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(y)={{field-2}}
$$

where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(y)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{y}.$

Let's denote

$$
P(x,y)={y}^{3},\,Q(x,y)=xy.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\,{{field-3}}
$$

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\,{{field-4}}
$$

Since for this equation 

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})={{field-5}},
$$

which depends on $y$ only, then an integrating factor for our equation is

$$
I(y)={{field-6}}.
$$

and we arrive at the exact equation

$$
{{field-7}}.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=h(y)
$$

where $h(y)$ is independent of $x,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(y)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(-\int h(y)\,\text{d}y)
$$

where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(y)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{y}.$

Let's denote

$$
P(x,y)={y}^{3},\,Q(x,y)=xy.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3})=3{y}^{2} \\ \frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)=y\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x}) & =\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}(3{y}^{2}-y) \\  & =3{y}^{-1}-{y}^{-2},\end{aligned}
$$

is a function of $y$ only, we can conclude that an integrating factor for our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(y) & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int -(3{y}^{-1}-{y}^{-2})\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(-(3\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1/y)) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡{y}^{-3})\cdot \operatorname{exp}⁡(-1/y) \\  & ={y}^{-3}\,{e}^{-1/y}.\end{aligned}
$$

and by multiplying our differential equation by the integrating factor, we have

$$
I(y)\cdot ({y}^{3}\,\text{d}x+xy\,\text{d}y)=I(y)\cdot 0
$$

which simplifies as

$$
{y}^{-3}{e}^{-1/y}({y}^{3}\,\text{d}x+xy\,\text{d}y)=0.
$$
